technique: withholding — what the poem refuses to name or explain, and why that works
poem:
The barn door hangs where you left it, half-swung
on the one hinge that still bites, neither shut
against the coming cold nor open to it,
waiting on a hand to decide the matter.
Frost has stiffened the grass to a gray felt,
each blade holding its crook of ice a while
before the sun, come late over the ridge now,
unmakes it to plain wet and lets it stand.
You stand too, in the doorway's halfway light,
counting what the season still asks of you —
not the owing, just the work, the honest list,
the things not finished because they are yours to finish.

Cool air and bare ground, waiting for hands that know what to shape there —

So — up!
lesson: Today, we work on one thing. Withholding. Withholding means the poem leaves something out on purpose and does not explain it. Look at three spots, waiting on a hand to decide the matter. The poem never says whose hand or what the decision is. Counting what the season still asks of you. It never lists the actual chores. The things not finished because they are yours to finish. It never names one thing. This works in a plain way. When the poem skips the detail, your own mind fills it in. You picture your own unfinished work. You supply with the poem held back. Because the gap is empty, you put yourself into it. A full list would push your own life out. Try this. Write a poem about a task, but never name the task. Describe everything around it instead. The second time, listen for how all that held back work pushes toward the last line, so up.
